items.title: Exploring File Uploads and Downloads in MCP
items.excerpt: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) started out as a simple way to connect models to tools, and that principle is still very much at its heart. Over the past two years, the things people build with the protocol have become more ambitious. Much more ambitious. Many of those MCP server projects now need to work with files - often driven by increasing agent capabilities and autonomy. Saving a PDF from a conversation to cloud storage and pulling a CSV into a sandbox have become very common requests from developers adopting MCP. Today, implementing these scenarios would require a bunch of bespoke tool conventions and transfer mechanisms - not something we’d want folks doing over and over. Because this request kept coming up in customer discussions, we bootstapped the File Uploads Working Group. We’ve spent the last month working through what a solution could look like. Thanks to the effort of our community and developers, we now have a rough extension definition, and we’d love for you to poke at it as we start prototyping and trying out how it works in the wild. Read the draft extension → Where the work stands#The work on the extension is still very much an experimental effort - while we have the shape outlined, we’re not sure yet that what we started with is what we’ll end up with. The best way to find out is, you guessed it - contact with reality. You might also notice that there’s no reference implementation yet - that’s because we expect that a lot of the inner workings will, in fact, be quite different once we start integrating our experiment with third-party file services, such as cloud storage, database import/export, and many others that require file input and output. As with all other extensions, this one will remain optional - there is no work required on either clients or servers if they don’t plan to support it (although we hope they really will, given the broad interest in this work). We expect to finalize the extension and have it become stable before the end

items.title: A More Predictable Release Cycle for MCP
items.excerpt: We’ve spent a lot of time over the past two years talking about ways to improve MCP, add new features and capabilities, and get on a more predictable release cadence. Clearly, there has been no shortage of ideas both from the maintainer and broader developer community. Getting those ideas reviewed, implemented, tested, and into a release is a whole other part of the job, and we want to make that specific part easier to follow for our community. For folks working on proposals, that means knowing when reviews will happen and how much time there is to make adjustments. SDK maintainers also need to know when the spec will stop changing - both client and server developers use our developer toolchain as a starting point to try new MCP capabilities out and share feedback. To make this process easier, we’re setting up a more consistent timeline for upcoming spec changes so that you don’t have to piece a schedule together from meeting notes and GitHub threads. The Core Maintainers worked through these questions together at MCPCon Europe, and Kurtis Van Gent recently wrote up the process in SEP-3398: Release Cycle Updates - this is our de facto release guidance moving forward. As a result of this work, we’re moving MCP specification releases to a regular six-month schedule. Two releases a year#We’ll generally publish specification releases on the last Tuesday of March and September. Alongside each release date, we’ll share the proposal deadlines and SDK beta dates, so you can work backward from them when planning your own implementation and testing. For the next release, we’re targeting March 30, 2027 - expect MCP version 2027-03-30 to land then. To keep that schedule predictable, a proposal that isn’t ready will move to a later release rather than delay the whole spec. Its authors can keep working on it without having to rush, and everyone else can continue preparing for the release they planned around. Note This changes how we prepare a release, not MCP messages or version

items.title: Issue types and fields are available for personal accounts
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Issue types and issue fields are now generally available on repositories owned by personal accounts. This brings the same planning capabilities to individual developers and open source maintainers to standardize your workflows and organize issues across repositories. Get started with issue types and issue fields Customize issue types: You can customize issue types from your personal account settings on the Issue types page under “Planning”. The defaults are Bug, Task, and Feature. You can customize them and create up to 25 issue types. Customize issue fields: You can customize issue fields from your personal account settings on the Issue fields page under “Planning”. The default issue fields are Priority, Effort, Start date, and Target date. You can customize them and create up to 25 issue fields, with support for text, number, date, single-select, and multi-select fields. You can also pin fields to issue types or make them available on issues without a type. Apply them to issues: You can set the issue type and fields when creating an issue or viewing an existing issue. You can also use them in projects to create custom views and perform bulk updates. Use the API to automate: You can use the REST and GraphQL APIs and webhooks to programmatically manage issue types and fields. Learn more about managing issue types and managing issue fields. Create labels and milestones from an issue You can now create labels and milestones directly from an issue, without navigating to the repository’s labels or milestones pages. If a label or milestone doesn’t match your search criteria, you’ll be prompted to create one. Join the discussion within GitHub Community. The post Issue types and fields are available for personal accounts appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: A minor GitHub planning feature, issue types and fields, now available for personal accounts. It has limited impact since our work mostly happens in org repos.

items.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
items.author: brownrout
items.excerpt: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.Here's a quick demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFfbXAwRq98Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful
items.why_it_matters: An open-source, on-device meeting transcription app. It is a niche productivity tool, though it shows how practical small local models have become.

items.title: AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.excerpt: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo. The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud, for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloudCodex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites —

items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
items.excerpt: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to re

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.excerpt: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon": { "type": "yes_no", "probability": 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot": { "type": "yes_no", "probability": 0.9234055387792485 }, "france": { "type": "yes_no", "probability": 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa": { "type": "yes_no", "probability": 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai, generative-ai, gemini, llm-release, jev, decision-models
items.why_it_matters: Google launched Gemini Decision 1, a cheap multimodal model for yes/no, choice and rubric questions. It compares directly with Jev and OpenAI's decision model, and fits classification and eval features we build for clients.

items.title: llm 0.37.2
items.excerpt: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w. LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1. Tags: projects, security, llm, releases
